description: Team Ceynova brings together science, data engineering, web development and design to turn NASA lunar data into an intuitive tool for comparing landing sites
summary: A lunar landing site is also a choice about time: when sunlight reaches the spacecraft, how long darkness lasts, and when Earth is visible. Ceynova brings these questions into one browser-based navigator. Using NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides, NASA LOLA topography and the NASA–JAXA SLDEM2015 elevation model, it calculates Sun and Earth visibility above the local terrain horizon. Users can explore 27 curated sites, see the sky from the surface, compare locations or arrival dates, and inspect continuous visibility windows and outages. A guided planner checks user-defined visibility requirements and builds a surface-operations schedule. Cautious and optimistic readings expose the effect of assumed terrain margins, while missing data remains identified. By connecting a Moon map, a local skyline and a mission timeline, Ceynova helps engineering teams, educators and the public understand the consequences of lunar site and date choices. Its results describe geometric visibility, with solar-input estimates provided separately as an educational illustration.
details:
Detailed Project Description

Why the landing date matters as much as the location

Before choosing a lunar landing site, a team needs to answer a practical question: will the Sun and Earth remain visible when the spacecraft needs them?

Near the lunar south pole, sunlight arrives at shallow angles. A distant crater rim can hide the Sun, and the terrain can interrupt a direct view of Earth. Moving to another location or changing the arrival date changes how those obstructions line up with the sky.

An average visibility percentage cannot describe that sequence. The same total sunlight can be distributed across many short windows or interrupted by one long darkness period. Those patterns have different implications for energy storage and surface operations. A mission therefore needs to be evaluated as a particular location, start date and duration.

Ceynova: Lunar landing site navigator was built to make that relationship visible. It lets users move from a view of the Moon to the sky above a site, then follow the consequences through an entire surface stay

What Team Ceynova built

Ceynova is a working browser application organised around four questions.

The catalogue contains 27 curated sites: ten with 20 m terrain profiles and seventeen in a nominal 60 m terrain tier. It includes historical landing locations, modern robotic missions, south-polar candidates and exploration regions elsewhere on the Moon. Custom coordinates are also supported. If terrain cannot be obtained for a custom point, the app explicitly labels its smooth-Moon fallback as Geometric.

Simple and Science views let users choose how much detail to see. Short explainers and three game challenges make the same calculations accessible to learners. The following sections explain how the data become the views and decisions shown in these workspaces.

Placing a site on the Moon and looking into its sky

The model begins with a site's latitude and east-positive longitude, obtained from cited landing records or candidate-site datasets. These coordinates locate the observer on a spherical lunar reference surface of radius R = 1737.4 km

For latitude φ and longitude λ, the outward unit vector is

û = (cos φ cos λ, cos φ sin λ, sin φ)

The observer's position is then

r_site = (R + h) û

Here, h is ground elevation plus observer height, expressed in kilometres to match R. The default planner uses an observer 2 m above the local ground. This connects the selected coordinates to the Moon's geometry and establishes the viewpoint used for the scientific calculations.

NASA/JPL's SPICE system supplies Sun and Earth positions and the Moon's orientation. The Python pipeline stores the resulting Moon-centred vectors every 30 minutes in the Moon's mean-Earth frame, MOON_ME. The browser uses cubic interpolation between samples, allowing the clock and sky to move continuously. Available years are 1969–1972, 2019 and 2024–2040.

A body must be viewed from the observer's location, so the site position is subtracted:

v(t) = r_body(t) − r_site

Using local east, north and up unit vectors, its sky position becomes

a(t) = atan2(v · ê, v · n̂)

e(t) = arcsin((v · û) / ‖v‖)

Azimuth a is the compass bearing, measured clockwise from north; elevation e is the angle above the local horizontal. Azimuth is wrapped to 0°–360°. Trigonometric calculations use radians, with displayed angles converted to degrees.

Subtracting the site position accounts for parallax, the difference between a view from the Moon's centre and a view from its surface. The resulting angles drive the Sun and Earth positions in Site Sky, the sky-path plot and the numerical readouts. The visual display and the visibility calculations therefore share the same observer geometry.

Turning lunar topography into the terrain skyline

Knowing a body's elevation is insufficient if a ridge stands in the way. Ceynova builds a terrain horizon profile: the highest obstruction angle in each compass direction as seen from the observer.

The input is a digital elevation model, a grid of measured ground heights. Polar profiles use NASA LOLA products; most non-polar profiles use SLDEM2015, which combines NASA LOLA measurements with JAXA Kaguya Terrain Camera data. IM-1 and Peak near Cabeus B use the broader LOLA south-polar model.

For each bundled site, the horizon engine examines 720 directions, spaced 0.5° apart, out to 150 km. It follows the curved lunar surface and samples the terrain along each direction.

For terrain height z at surface distance d, its apparent elevation is

ψ(d, θ) = atan2((R + z) cos(d / R) − (R + z₀), (R + z) sin(d / R))

Here, θ is the compass direction and z₀ is ground elevation at the site plus the observer height. All distances and heights in this equation use the same unit. The horizon in that direction is the largest sampled obstruction:

H(θ) = max_{d ≤ 150 km} ψ(d, θ)

This is why a distant mountain can matter: it may produce the highest obstruction even when the nearby ground is clear. Including lunar curvature prevents distant terrain from being treated as though it lies on a flat plane.

The resulting H(θ) becomes the skyline drawn in Site Sky and the obstruction used to calculate rise and set events. Missing terrain samples retain a data-gap flag.

Figure 1. Site Sky at Shackleton rim. The gold line is the terrain horizon from NASA LOLA 20 m data; the timeline shows when the Sun, Earth and both together are visible over a 14-day window.

The 60 m tier describes nominal source fidelity. SLDEM2015 patches use approximately 59 m spacing nearby and 118 m beyond 30 km. Neither tier resolves individual rocks or landing-pad hazards. NASA's CGI Moon Kit supplies the globe's colour and elevation-derived visual shading; that visual slope texture is separate from the terrain-horizon analysis and is not used to judge landing steepness.

Finding visibility windows and continuous outages

The Sun and Earth appear as discs, rather than mathematical points. Their apparent angular radius is

α(t) = arcsin(R_body / ‖v(t)‖)

Ceynova compares the upper edge of the disc with the terrain skyline at the same bearing:

c(t) = e(t) + α(t) − H(a(t))

The clearance c answers a direct question: how far above or below the obstruction is the body's upper edge? A positive value means at least part of the disc is above the modelled skyline; it does not mean the full disc is unobstructed.

Because terrain models have finite resolution, the app applies an explicit angular margin m:

  • Clear: c(t) > m
  • Marginal: −m ≤ c(t) ≤ m
  • Blocked: c(t) < −m

The current margins are 0.25° for 20 m terrain, 0.4° for the 60 m tier, 0.5° for 80 m terrain and 0.05° for the geometric fallback. These are modelling assumptions, not calibrated confidence intervals or guaranteed bounds.

For a mission window of duration T, let T_C be Clear time and T_M be Marginal time. The two reported visibility fractions are

F_cautious = T_C / T ,   F_optimistic = (T_C + T_M) / T

The cautious reading counts only Clear time. The optimistic reading also includes Marginal time. Applying the same rule to both bodies identifies periods when both Sun and Earth are visible.

The engine refines state-transition times, joins adjacent intervals and calculates the longest continuous window and outage. For the cautious Sun reading,

D_{max, cautious} = max_j (b_j − a_j)

where each [a_j, b_j] is a continuous period without Clear Sun visibility inside the selected mission window. An outage that extends beyond the window is measured only for the portion inside it.

These calculations produce the timeline strips, longest-darkness value, Earth-blackout duration and event jumps. If scientific coverage is incomplete, the affected whole-window metrics remain unavailable; missing time is not silently counted as visible or blocked.

Figure 2. Evaluate results for Malapert massif: the site meets the example limits, with 84% Sun above the terrain horizon and a longest darkness of 42 h 19 min.

Turning visibility results into mission choices

The Mission Planner starts with user-defined requirements. For example, the editable 14-day CLPS lander preset assumes at least 65% Sun visibility, no more than 48 hours of continuous darkness and at least 50% Earth visibility.

In general, a direct-to-Earth scenario passes when

F_Sun ≥ F_{Sun, min} ,   D_{Sun, max} ≤ D_allowed ,   F_Earth ≥ F_{Earth, min}

The thresholds are the user's assumptions, not NASA-approved spacecraft specifications. The app evaluates complete scenarios as follows:

  • Confirmed: every active requirement passes using cautious values.
  • Possible: the requirements pass only when optimistic values are allowed.
  • Fail: at least one active requirement fails even on the optimistic reading.

Within the same outcome class, a chosen planning priority orders candidate sites. The balanced preference uses

S = 0.35 F_{Sun, c} + 0.30 F_{Earth, c} + 0.35 F_{Both, c}

where the fractions are cautious values between 0 and 1. Power- and communications-oriented preferences use different weights. This score expresses a preference among visibility results; it is not a physical measure of overall site quality.

Compare keeps one scenario fixed while changing the site or start date in the other. Timelines align by elapsed mission time so users can see the consequences of the change. The Delay Explorer repeats the analysis across a year of candidate surface-operation start dates.

Figure 3. Compare and the Delay Explorer for Malapert massif. Across a year of start dates, the cautious Sun share for a 14-day stay ranges from 0% to 100%.

The planner's year strip screens Sun visibility and cautious longest darkness. Earth visibility is checked separately for candidate windows where available; an unchecked Earth result remains unresolved. These are candidate touchdown and surface-operation dates, not orbital launch windows.

Figure 4. Mission Planner, Sites step: 12 south-polar sites ranked against example robotic-mission limits (7 Confirmed, 5 Fail), with the results shown on the MoonFigure 5. Year-long touchdown search for Malapert massif: 154 Confirmed days, with the top three windows.

For a selected window, the planner assembles a schedule with four geometric states: both bodies visible, Sun only, Earth only, and neither. These support suggested activities such as local work, telemetry or hibernation. The user can copy a Markdown brief containing the requirements, results and a link that restores the plan.

Figure 6. Surface operations schedule for the top window, split into operating states with critical events.

Connecting sunlight to an illustrative solar-input estimate

A visible Sun does not determine electrical output by itself. Panel area, efficiency, orientation and Sun distance also matter. Ceynova's optional solar-input panel demonstrates these relationships using

P(t) = I₀ (1 AU / d_Sun(t))² A η max(0, cos i(t))

Here, I₀ = 1361 W/m² is the reference solar irradiance at 1 AU, A is panel area in square metres, η is efficiency, and i is the angle between the panel's outward normal and the Sun. The inverse-square term accounts for distance; the cosine term accounts for panel pointing.

For a horizontal panel, the incidence factor is cos i = sin e. This explains an important polar engineering issue: the Sun can be visible while illuminating a horizontal panel at a poor angle.

Energy is integrated over the selected visibility intervals:

E = ∫_V P(t) dt

With time measured in hours, the result is in watt-hours. The cautious estimate integrates Clear intervals; the optimistic estimate adds Marginal intervals. The implementation uses numerical integration with Simpson's rule.

The panel lets users explore orientation, area and efficiency. It is labelled illustrative solar input because it omits dust, temperature-dependent efficiency, electrical losses, spacecraft loads, self-shadowing and partial-disc shading. It does not provide a mission power forecast, and its energy estimate is separate from the planner's visibility-based classifications.

Why this approach is useful

For engineering teams, Ceynova makes the sequence of opportunities and interruptions available for discussion. A long continuous outage becomes visible alongside the percentage that might otherwise conceal it. Changing a requirement, location or date exposes the trade-off.

For educators and students, the app connects spherical coordinates, vectors, terrain geometry, solar incidence and constraint checking to one interactive problem. Users can inspect why a result changes instead of only receiving a verdict.

For the public, the first-person skyline gives meaning to numbers that are difficult to interpret on a map. A low Sun passing behind a ridge explains the result directly.

The creative choice is to connect geographic location, the observer's sky and mission time through one calculation foundation. The learning tools and planning views therefore show the same underlying geometry. Ceynova runs in a browser without login or installation, and previously loaded assets can be cached for offline use.
Making this possible in a browser-based tool relied heavily on NASA’s extensive, openly documented datasets and ephemeris tools, which enabled rapid prototyping and rigorous cross-checking without proprietary software.

Evidence behind the calculations

The scientific calculation was checked in separate layers.

The Product 69 comparison is not exact agreement. Sun-centre visibility at Mons Mouton is 45.05% against the reference pixel's 45.10%, while Peak near Shackleton differs by about 29.6 percentage points. Reference periods, terrain resolution and visibility definitions differ; neighbouring reference pixels also vary substantially near ridges. Those discrepancies are retained in the repository reports.

The small positional errors establish neither landing safety nor equivalent accuracy for terrain obstruction angles. The code also has automated tests for geometry, intervals, metrics, constraints and data-gap handling, with reproducible validation reports available in the source repository.

Design decisions and present limits

The architecture separates data preparation from browser interaction. Python prepares the astronomical tables and terrain horizons; TypeScript calculates local geometry and mission intervals. Background Web Workers handle calculations, while WebGL2 and Canvas draw the views. This keeps the interactive experience connected to inspectable numerical code.

Several limits determine how the results should be interpreted. The default planner uses a fixed 2 m observer: entering another mast height currently records an assumption without regenerating the horizon. Catalogue coordinates retain their verification labels and require independent checking. Selecting a relay relaxes the direct-to-Earth visibility requirement without modelling a relay network.

Ceynova does not score landing slope or surface hazards, calculate radio-link budgets, or predict thermal survival. The Earth-to-Moon flight view is schematic, and its transit time is a user assumption. Uncached data and custom-terrain requests require connectivity; custom terrain also depends on service availability.

Next priorities are independent coordinate verification, broader terrain and event validation, calibrated uncertainty margins, recalculation for user-entered observer heights, reliable custom-terrain delivery, and usability testing with unaided users and physical phones.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Our team used Claude (including Claude Code), Google Gemini, OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT to support development, including pipeline scaffolding, UI and WebGL shader implementation, unit testing and debugging.

All architectural decisions, engineering assumptions, dataset selections and technical justifications were made and critically evaluated by team members. No generative AI runs within the live application. All runtime results are calculated deterministically using numerical algorithms and source datasets, with comparisons generated through predefined text templates.

AI-assisted code was manually reviewed and validated through automated tests, terrain consistency checks and cross-validation against recorded JPL Horizons data.

Official, unedited NASA imagery was used for Moon and Earth textures. Other scene elements and styling were developed using AI-assisted graphics code and are labelled illustrative. No NASA logos or mission insignia were AI-generated or altered. Any separate demonstration media includes appropriate tool attribution.
